I've been writing a novel for quite a few years now (I have issues with just sitting down and getting it done. Hope to see some kind of /v/shutupandwrite subverse get created) and in my mind I've labeled it as YAFiction. The thing is, I'm not entirely sure what YAFiction is.

I have a rudimentary idea of what the genre entails. For example, I believe it lacks graphic sexual content (so sexual intercourse and violence of a sexual nature are implied and occur "off-screen," if they occur at all). I also feel that the writing is more....juvenile (for lack of a better word). When I read YA Fiction, it feels more light and air-y - more like "brain candy," if you will, than adult fiction novels. It may be the lack of political intrigue - not that YA Fiction lacks political intrigue, but it seems more simple when compared to the politics involved in books like Melanie Rawn's Dragon Prince.

I'm interested in hearing how others define YA Fiction!
What IS YA Fiction? How does it differ from regular (e.g., "adult") fiction?

Tbh I think the main difference between YA and adult fiction is the age of the protagonist. YAs usually focus on characters age 12-18, while adult fiction goes from 20s on up. YA are more likely to censor violence or include an obvious romance subplot, at least in my experience, and are typically shorter, but none of that is a hard and fast rule. There are some stories that tackle harder, darker subjects in more mature ways in YA novels, and there are some very light, simplistic adult novels.
You know, I hadn't even considered the age of the protagonist. You're absolutely right!

I always figured that 'adult' fiction dealt with more mature or grown-up stuff that younger people don't or shouldn't have to deal with. These would be more visceral, crude aspects of life that younger generations should not be exposed to in order to protect the little innocense they have left. Examples could be having to run out the hospital, shouting at complete strangers, looking for an organ donor for their dying relative inside that hospital. The desperation and hopelessness is visceral and palpable. Another example would be for a young man (maybe in his 30s), having to dress his father for his funeral, and sadly, having to don on him a new suit he was planning to give him on his birthday. Tragic scenes like these you would not want to find in young adult fiction. In young adult fiction I would expect to find themes of conquering obstacles and small triumphs that enable the character to grow. Basically, themes a teenager or young adult would identify with, like overcoming obstacles, self discovery, adventure, fantasy, etc. Adult fiction can be unapologetically boring too, dabbling too much in useless details or nuances like a jilted ex-lover's long bouts of introspection, or painstaking detail about formal dinner protocols of high society, etc. Young adult cannot afford to be boring, so it has to be fun to read and needs to keep the story moving. That's why War and Peace is 5 inches thick... nobody ever told the author to keep the story moving LOL

Uh oh. My YA novel includes quite a bit of "dark" experiences that I'm sure fall into the categories you've listed. I agree with you about the focus on keeping the plot moving forward, perhaps at the expense of fully providing an immersively thorough description of the setting(s).

Dark is fantastic, don't you worry. I've found that YA can deliver some really dark and serious themes in a way that most other books fail to. Like Zeref says, it's not really bound by what age it is meant for, as long as you can do it well, but that applies to anything really.
